analysis.one_liner: Phases out production of ozone-destroying chemicals like CFCs within five years.
analysis.headline: Sen. Al Gore's bill to phase out CFCs and other ozone-depleting chemicals within five years, introduced with one cosponsor on May 1, 1989, was referred to the Senate environment committee and never received another action before the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the EPA to list chemicals that destroy the stratospheric ozone layer — starting with CFC-11, CFC-12, CFC-113, halon-1211, halon-1301 and carbon tetrachloride — and then cut their production step by step, reaching zero within five years except for medical uses. It would also have banned use of the chemicals in interstate commerce (with a carve-out for servicing household appliances until 2005), barred imports from countries lacking equally strict programs, required 99% destruction of the chemicals at disposal, and set civil and criminal penalties plus citizen-suit rights. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be the general public: by eliminating production and release of ozone-depleting chemicals, the bill aimed to slow depletion of the stratospheric ozone layer, which filters ultraviolet radiation linked to skin cancer and cataracts [S2][S3]. People would also benefit from rules requiring that the chemicals not be vented and that refrigerators and air conditioners be drained and destroyed at licensed facilities rather than dumped [S3]. Chemical companies that developed safe substitute chemicals stood to gain a new market, and the bill required those companies to file health and safety studies before commercial introduction [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Would have cut production of the most dangerous ozone-depleting chemicals — CFC-11, CFC-12, CFC-113, halon-1211, halon-1301 and carbon tetrachloride — to zero within five years, faster than the phaseout schedules in force at the time.

Would have banned venting of listed chemicals and required refrigerators, air conditioners and foam products to be disposed of only with 99% destruction of the chemicals, keeping them out of the atmosphere.
Would have barred imports of listed chemicals and products made with them from countries without equally strict reduction programs, preventing companies from simply moving production abroad.
Gave the EPA authority to speed up the phaseout further if new science showed it necessary or substitutes made it attainable, and let citizens sue violators or force EPA action after 60 days' notice.

analysis.who_pays: Producers of the listed chemicals — CFCs, halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform and others — would lose their markets on a fixed statutory clock: production capped at 1986 levels after one year, 75% after two, 50% after three, 5% after four, and zero (except medical uses) after five [S3]. Makers and servicers of refrigerators, air conditioners and other equipment would bear retooling, leak-proof servicing and licensed-disposal costs, some of which would reach consumers in prices [S3]. Importers and retailers of goods made using these chemicals would lose access to those products unless exporting countries matched U.S. limits, and violators faced civil penalties up to $25,000 per violation per day and criminal penalties of up to two years' imprisonment [S3].

drawbacks.text: The five-year phaseout was set in statute with fixed deadlines based on 1986 production levels; EPA could speed the schedule up but had no authority to slow it down if substitute chemicals or equipment were not ready, which could have caused supply disruptions and price spikes for refrigeration and air-conditioning.

Consumers would pay some of the cost: appliances would be accepted for disposal only at licensed facilities after the chemicals were removed and destroyed, and products made using listed chemicals could be barred from import, raising prices for appliances and some imported goods.

The import ban, conditioned on the EPA Administrator certifying that foreign countries ran programs at least as strict as U.S. law, went beyond what trade agreements of the era plainly allowed and risked trade disputes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case was strong — ozone depletion was understood at the time as a hazard that compounds over time and cannot be safely reversed — and the bill contained real accommodations for genuine needs: medical uses with no safe substitute, servicing of existing household appliances until 2005, and a presidential national-security exemption for halon fire extinguishants with a Defense Department mandate to stop emitting halons in equipment testing [S2][S3]. The honest cost is that the five-year deadline was aggressive and legally rigid: if substitutes had lagged, the appliance and refrigeration sectors — and their customers — would have absorbed sharp transition costs, with no statutory mechanism to delay. On balance the bill traded a known, compounding environmental hazard for temporary industry transition costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and never received another recorded action — no hearing, no vote — before that Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Sen. Al Gore introduced the bill on May 1, 1989; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
One Senate Democrat signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee took no further action, and the bill died there when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Producers of CFCs and halons, and the appliance, refrigeration and fire-suppression businesses built on those chemicals, avoided a mandatory five-year production cutoff and the retooling, servicing and disposal mandates; because the bill never reached a vote, no senator had to take a position on it.

for.name: Sen. Albert Gore, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote the five-year phaseout, import restrictions and disposal mandates into it.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee (chaired by Sen. Quentin Burdick, D-ND)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 1, 1989 and took no further recorded action on it for the remaining twenty months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken on the bill, so no partisan split is recorded; its only two supporters of record, the sponsor and one cosponsor, were both Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would have capped their production at 1986 levels within a year and cut it to zero within five years, except for FDA-approved medical uses — eliminating the market for their core products. Their interest in keeping production going ran directly against protecting the ozone layer.

They would have had to redesign products for a totally enclosed, serviceable charge, stop venting during service, and route old appliances to licensed disposal with 99% destruction — significant costs, though the bill let them keep using the chemicals to service existing appliances until 2005.

Halon-1211 and halon-1301 were on the priority list, but the President could exempt national-security sites for up to a year at a time, and the Pentagon was ordered to stop releasing halons during fire-equipment testing — a partial carve-out for its largest user.

The bill declared a national policy of replacing listed chemicals with safe alternatives and required EPA to identify and clear replacements, creating a market for substitute refrigerants and processes — while forcing those producers to disclose health and safety studies first.
